query: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small amount of titanium (Ti) into the near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst can address the combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use.
generation.intervention: Introduction of a small amount of titanium (Ti)
generation.conditions: Transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of ordered precipitates (e.g., L12 or B2-type) under appropriate heat treatments
generation.mechanism: Pronounced lattice distortion (solid-solution strengthening) and the formation of ordered precipitates, which can impede dislocation motion effectively while a ductile FCC matrix is retained
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use
generation.baseline: Unmodified near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst
generation.boundary: Transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of titanium (Ti) to be introduced and the optimal heat treatment conditions are uncertain

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the performance of the modified catalyst with the unmodified catalyst under transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified catalyst does not show improved performance compared to the unmodified catalyst, the hypothesis is falsified

Benefiting from the so-called “high-entropy effect,” MPEAs can circumvent limitations imposed by the traditional Gibbs phase rule, often stabilizing simple solid-solution phases. Coupled with pronounced lattice-distortion effects, these characteristics can yield superior mechanical properties [,,,,,], creating new avenues for materials design.
A milestone was reached in 2004 with the proposal of the equiatomic Fe-Co-Cr-Ni-Mn “Cantor” alloy [,], which forms a single face-centered cubic (FCC) phase and exhibits exceptional strength, ductility, and fracture toughness at cryogenic temperatures. However, its outstanding performance is largely confined to low-temperature regimes, limiting room-temperature applicability. Subsequent research has therefore focused on developing equiatomic solid-solution variants and non-equiatomic derivatives of the Cantor system to enhance room-temperature mechanical properties. Nonetheless, the vast compositional space of MPEAs, encompassing tens of thousands of possible elemental combinations, renders traditional empirical trial-and-error approaches increasingly inefficient, particularly regarding development time and cost. There is a pressing need for efficient design strategies that minimize experimental iterations and accelerate the discovery of new MPEAs. The rapid advancement of machine learning (ML) offers a powerful solution. Fueled by progress in computational tools, alloy design is transitioning from trial-and-error exploration towards demand-driven, property-oriented design—a key driver of modern industrial innovation.
